packs.title: Pages & City Paths
packs.promise: Turn Dublin’s objects, pictures and public places into small discoveries of your own.

q.s: Pack an imaginary journey using three real objects.
st: Choose a small everyday object from an accessible display. Read its label before deciding what it might do in your imaginary travel kit.
Find two more objects with different jobs: carrying, fastening, making, eating or another practical purpose. Keep the objects in their cases.
For each, record its labeled identity and your invented use on the journey. Say when your idea goes beyond the label.
Give your three-object kit one limitation. What would you still be unable to do?

q.s: Give two details in a painting a beginning, a change and an ending.
st: Choose a painting you can comfortably spend a few minutes with. Find two details that could belong in one story: an object and a shadow, a figure and a doorway, or something else you notice.
Write a first line that connects the details. In a second line, let something change.
Give the story a third line that ends it. Keep it short enough to read in one breath.
Mark the three lines as your fiction. Add the painting’s title from its label so you can find it again.

q.s: Put a printing process back in order.
st: Use the labels to find something involved in arranging letters or an image, something that presses an impression and something connected with the finished page.
Arrange your three finds in a written production sequence. Explain one job each performs.
Choose a hand-off between two stages. What has to be ready before the next stage can work?
If a stage is not on display, mark the gap and fill it from the museum’s guide, clearly identifying that source.

packs.title: Liberties in Detail
packs.promise: Find reading nooks, street rhythms and small design ideas across the Liberties.

q.s: Let three writers change the way you group a small collection.
st: Choose two portraits whose accompanying words give you a connection: a kind of writing, a date or another stated detail.
Put your grouping rule into one sentence. You do not need to recognize either writer beforehand.
Find a third plaque. Use one fact on it to broaden, narrow or replace your rule.
Record the three names and the rule you ended with. If a plaque is hard to read, use a clear example rather than guessing.

q.s: Give two window finds a shared imaginary home.
st: Choose two displayed objects that seem to have different practical uses.
For each, note one visible design detail: a curve, material, handle, pattern or scale.
Invent a room in which both objects belong. Explain how the two details help them work together.
Give the room a purpose rather than a price. Leave the objects exactly where they are.

q.s: Make a small woven pattern from the shapes around you.
st: Choose two repeated forms you can see in the park: perhaps a row of slats and a line of paving.
Draw three lines in one direction and three across them, or describe that simple grid in words.
At each crossing, alternate which line goes over and which goes under. Give the two line families different colors or names.
Change one part of the repeating pattern, then explain where the rhythm breaks. Keep the result as your own small design.
